added: A reflected ceiling plan (RCP) is a drawing that shows which shows the items are located on the ceiling of a room or space. It is referred to as a reflected ceiling plan since it is drawn to display a view of the ceiling as if it was reflected onto a mirror on the floor.

#Pretend that you are hovering a couple of feet above the ceiling.<ref>https://www.edrawsoft.com/reflectedceiling-design-guide.php</ref> [[Image:Read a Reflected Ceiling Plan Step 1 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#Imagine that the ceiling below you is transparent (see-through).[[Image:Read a Reflected Ceiling Plan Step 2 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#Visualize the ceiling over the floor below.[[Image:Read a Reflected Ceiling Plan Step 3 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#Read a reflected ceiling plan using this concept.[[Image:Read a Reflected Ceiling Plan Step 4 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Notice how the reflected ceiling plan relates to the floor plan.<ref>https://www.edrawsoft.com/reflectedceiling-design-guide.php</ref> [[Image:Read a Reflected Ceiling Plan Step 5 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#Observe the relationship of light fixtures to the furniture below.[[Image:Read a Reflected Ceiling Plan Step 6.jpg|center]]

#*In some cases, the items below are not shown, in order to keep the RCP
from becoming too confusing.
#*When furniture, fixtures or the millwork below are shown,they are shown dotted.

#Understand the information. An RCP should contain the following:<ref>https://www.northernarchitecture.us/building-codes/reflected-ceiling-plan.html</ref> [[Image:Read a Reflected Ceiling Plan Step 7.jpg|center]]
#*The construction of the ceiling (gypsum board., acoustical tile, etc)
#*A specification and/or finish (paint, stucco, etc.) of the ceiling material
#*The height of the ceiling above the finished floor (A.F.F.)
#*Dimensions
#*A legend explaining the symbols on the RCP

#*An explanation of any ceiling features such as bulkheads, soffits,
raised or vaulted areas, trim or decorative applications
#*Section symbols to further explain the construction of any ceiling features

#Look for special ceiling features on the RCP, such as:<ref>https://www.northernarchitecture.us/building-codes/reflected-ceiling-plan.html</ref> [[Image:Read a Reflected Ceiling Plan Step 8.jpg|center]]
#*Speakers from a stereo or other communication device
#*Emergency lighting, exit signs
#*Security cameras or domes
#*[[Repair a Pop up Sprinkler Head|Sprinkler heads]]
#*Smoke or fire alarm devices

#*Return air grilles and supply air diffusers for the Heating,
Ventilating and Air Conditioning (HVAC) system
#*Exhaust fans
#*Seismic information and/ or details
#*Expansion joint information and/ or details
#Refer to the engineers electrical drawings for:<ref>https://cdn-web.iccsafe.org/wp-content/uploads/PR-Elec-Req.pdf</ref> [[Image:Read a Reflected Ceiling Plan Step 9 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#*Electrical wiring specifications
#*Circuitry layout
#*Connections to the electrical panel
#*Location of switches
== Tips ==
*A reflected ceiling plan layout must comply with local building codes, electrical codes as well as fire codes.
*Interior designers and architects draw reflected ceiling plans and then pass them to their consulting engineering firm. The electrical engineer then adds the electrical circuitry, etc.
*A reflected ceiling plan can be found in a set of construction drawings for a house or a retail store.
== Things You'll Need ==
*A drawing of a reflected ceiling plan and the floor plan that goes with it.

removed: A reflected ceiling plan (RCP) shows where items will be located on the ceiling of a room or space. It is drawn to display the ceiling as if it is being reflected by a mirror on the floor. Once you get the hang of looking at the RCP from the proper perspective, use the provided legend to identify the various symbols and abbreviations it contains. Utilize the RCP alongside its complementary floor plan (and, in some cases, electrical plan) to fully visualize the space.
===Visualizing the RCP Perspective===

#Picture yourself a few feet/meters above the ceiling in question. For instance, if you’re looking at an RCP for a first-floor living room, imagine that you’re standing in the upstairs bedroom right above it.<ref>https://www.lifeofanarchitect.com/architectural-graphics-101-number-01/</ref>[[Image:Read a Reflected Ceiling Plan Step 1 Version 3.jpg|center]]

#Imagine that you can see through the ceiling that’s below you. In other words, pretend that the ceiling is still there, but that you can see right through it. It’s as if the ceiling is transparent when looking at it from above, but not when looking at it from below.<ref>https://www.lifeofanarchitect.com/architectural-graphics-101-number-01/</ref>[[Image:Read a Reflected Ceiling Plan Step 2 Version 3.jpg|center]]
#*This is the same perspective you should imagine when looking at a floor plan. In fact, an RCP is at its most useful when used in combination with a coordinating floor plan.

#Envision the floor and everything on it as a big mirror. That is to say, the ceiling that’s there but is transparent to you is being reflected off of the floor—and you can see the reflection! This is the “reflected” part of a reflected ceiling plan.<ref>https://www.lifeofanarchitect.com/architectural-graphics-101-number-01/</ref>[[Image:Read a Reflected Ceiling Plan Step 3 Version 3.jpg|center]]
#*Using this mirrored reflection approach means that you can visualize the ceiling from the same overhead perspective—and at the same scale—as the coordinating floor plan.
#*Keep reminding yourself that the items you see are on the ceiling, not the floor. RCPs are extremely useful, but it’s easy to get confused if you forget how they work.
===Identifying RCP Components===

#Find the scale of the RCP to ensure it coordinates with other plans. Somewhere on the RCP, you should find a notation like the following: “Scale: 1/8 in = 1 ft.” In this case, every {{convert|0.125|in|mm|abbr=on}} on the drawing is equivalent to {{convert|1|ft|cm|abbr=on}} in the actual structure.<ref>https://www.northernarchitecture.us/building-codes/reflected-ceiling-plan.html</ref>[[Image:Read a Reflected Ceiling Plan Step 4 Version 3.jpg|center]]

#*If you’re using multiple plans, such as an RCP, floor plan, and electrical plan, make sure they’re all using the same scale. If they’re not, the task of coordinating the job will be far more difficult.

#Locate the legend to define RCP symbols and abbreviations. Any decent RCP will have a clearly-marked, boxed-in section labeled “Legend.” In this section, all of the symbols and abbreviations used in the RCP should be defined. The legend is particularly helpful because, unfortunately, the symbols and abbreviations used in RCPs are not universal.<ref>https://www.houseplanshelper.com/lighting-symbols.html</ref>[[Image:Read a Reflected Ceiling Plan Step 5 Version 3.jpg|center]]

#*For instance, recessed lights are sometimes symbolized by a simple circle, and at other times by a capital R inside a circle inside a square. Likewise, a ceiling fan sometimes looks like a fan with 4 blades, and other times is simply a circle with an X in its center.

#Use the legend to identify key ceiling features provided in the RCP. RCPs vary in the amount of ceiling components they reveal, based on the needs of the job and other factors. However, they typically provide many if not all of the following details:<ref>https://www.northernarchitecture.us/building-codes/reflected-ceiling-plan.html</ref>[[Image:Read a Reflected Ceiling Plan Step 6 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#*The construction material of the ceiling (gypsum board, acoustical tile, etc).
#*A specification and/or finish (paint, stucco, etc.) of the ceiling material.
#*The height of the ceiling above the finished floor (A.F.F.).
#*The ceiling’s dimensions (length, width).
#*An explanation of any ceiling features such as bulkheads, soffits, raised or vaulted areas, and trim or decorative applications.
#*Seismic information and/or details.
#*Expansion joint information and/or details.

#*Symbols that pinpoint the location of items such as light fixtures, power outlets and switches, speakers from a stereo or other communication device, emergency lighting and/or exit signs, security cameras or domes, sprinkler heads, smoke or fire alarm devices, return air grilles and supply air diffusers for the HVAC system, exhaust fans, and electrical wiring between fixtures (this isn’t shown in all RCPs).
===Using the RCP Alongside Other Plans===

#Compare the RCP to the floor plan that complements it. Look at the floor plan from the same perspective—above the ceiling, with the ceiling being transparent—but forget about the mirrored floor this time. Instead, imagine that you’re looking directly down onto the floor and whatever is on or slightly above it.<ref>https://www.lifeofanarchitect.com/architectural-graphics-101-number-01/</ref>[[Image:Read a Reflected Ceiling Plan Step 7 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#*The RCP and floor plan should be drawn at the exact same scale. Check the scale notation on the drawing to confirm this.

#*In some, but not all, RCPs, floor plan items (like furniture) appear in dashed lines, while ceiling items appear in full lines. In a coordinating floor plan, the dashed and full lines are reversed—that is, the ceiling fan symbol would be drawn with dashed lines.

#Refer to a separate electrical plan if wiring isn’t included in the RCP. Some RCPs show the wiring runs, junction boxes, switches, and so on. However, this can cause the RCP to become very cluttered, so this information may instead be provided in a separate electrical plan. This plan, like the RCP and floor plan, should be drawn to the same scale so that all 3 can be used in concert with each other. Use the legend on the electrical plan to identify items such as:<ref>https://cdn-web.iccsafe.org/wp-content/uploads/PR-Elec-Req.pdf</ref>[[Image:Read a Reflected Ceiling Plan Step 8 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#*Electrical wiring specifications.
#*Circuitry layout.
#*Connections to the electrical panel.
#*Location of switches.

#Make changes during the design phase by using the plans together. For example, looking at the floor plan and RCP side-by-side may lead you to relocate a ceiling light fixture so it better coordinates with the intended location for the couch. Similarly, referring to the electrical plan may convince you of the need to add more light switches based on the likely traffic patterns created by the furniture placement.<ref>https://www.lifeofanarchitect.com/architectural-graphics-101-number-01/</ref>[[Image:Read a Reflected Ceiling Plan Step 9 Version 3.jpg|center]]
#*It’s much easier and cheaper to make changes now, on paper, as opposed to when the structure is nearing completion.
== Tips ==
*Like other building plans, an RCP layout must comply with local building codes, electrical codes, and fire codes.

*Interior designers and architects draw reflected ceiling plans and then pass them to their consulting engineering firm. The electrical engineer then adds the electrical circuitry, etc, either on the RCP or in a separate electrical plan.

added: A reflected ceiling plan (RCP) is a combined architectural and engineering drawing which shows where items will be located on the ceiling of a room or space. It is referred to as a reflected ceiling plan because it is drawn to display a view of the ceiling as if it was reflected onto a mirror on the floor. Once you get the hang of looking at the RCP from the proper perspective, use the provided legend to identify the various symbols and abbreviations it contains. Utilize the RCP in concert with its complementary floor plan (and, in some cases, electrical plan) to fully visualize the space.
===Visualizing the RCP Perspective===

#Picture yourself a few feet/meters above the ceiling in question. For instance, if you’re looking at an RCP for a first-floor living room, imagine that you’re standing in the upstairs bedroom right above it.<ref>https://www.lifeofanarchitect.com/architectural-graphics-101-number-01/</ref>[[Image:Read a Reflected Ceiling Plan Step 1 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Imagine that you can see through the ceiling that’s below you. In other words, the ceiling is still there, but you can see right through it as if it’s transparent—or as if you have X-ray vision like Superman!<ref>https://www.lifeofanarchitect.com/architectural-graphics-101-number-01/</ref>[[Image:Read a Reflected Ceiling Plan Step 2 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#Envision the floor and everything on it as a big mirror. That is to say, the ceiling that’s there but is transparent to you is being reflected off of the floor—and you can see the reflection! This is the “reflected” part of a reflected ceiling plan.<ref>https://www.lifeofanarchitect.com/architectural-graphics-101-number-01/</ref>[[Image:Read a Reflected Ceiling Plan Step 3 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#*Using this mirrored reflection approach means that you can visualize the ceiling from the same overhead perspective—and at the same scale—as the coordinating floor plan.

#Remember that the items you see are on the ceiling, not the floor. RCPs are extremely useful, but it’s easy to get confused if you don’t keep reminding yourself how they work. Even though the drawing makes it look like the fixtures, wiring, architectural details, and so on are on the floor, they’re on the ceiling!<ref>https://www.lifeofanarchitect.com/architectural-graphics-101-number-01/</ref>[[Image:Read a Reflected Ceiling Plan Step 4 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#*RCPs are most useful when used in combination with a matching floor plan.
===Identifying RCP Components===

#Find the scale of the RCP to ensure it coordinates with other plans. Somewhere on the RCP, you should find a notation like the following: “Scale: 1/8 in = 1 ft.” In this case, every {{convert|0.125|in|mm|abbr=on}} on the drawing is equivalent to {{convert|1|ft|cm|abbr=on}} in the actual structure.<ref>https://www.northernarchitecture.us/building-codes/reflected-ceiling-plan.html</ref>

#*If you’re using multiple plans, such as an RCP, floor plan, and electrical plan, make sure they’re all using the same scale. If they’re not, the task of coordinating the job will be far more difficult.

#Locate the legend to define RCP symbols and abbreviations. Any decent RCP will have a clearly-marked, boxed-in section labeled “Legend.” In this section, all of the symbols and abbreviations used in the RCP should be defined. The legend is particularly helpful because, unfortunately, the symbols and abbreviations used in RCPs are not universal.<ref>https://www.houseplanshelper.com/lighting-symbols.html</ref>

#*For instance, recessed lights are sometimes symbolized by a simple circle, and at other times by a capital R inside a circle inside a square. Likewise, a ceiling fan sometimes looks like a fan with 4 blades, and other times is simply a circle with an X in its center.<ref>http://www.construction53.com/2011/09/blueprint-the-meaning-of-symbols/</ref>

#Use the legend to identify key details provided in the RCP. RCPs vary in the amount of components and detail they reveal, based on the needs of the job and other factors. However, they nearly always provide at least the following information:<ref>https://www.northernarchitecture.us/building-codes/reflected-ceiling-plan.html</ref>[[Image:Read a Reflected Ceiling Plan Step 7.jpg|center]]
#*The construction material of the ceiling (gypsum board, acoustical tile, etc).
#*A specification and/or finish (paint, stucco, etc.) of the ceiling material.
#*The height of the ceiling above the finished floor (A.F.F.).
#*The ceiling’s dimensions (length, width).
#*An explanation of any ceiling features such as bulkheads, soffits, raised or vaulted areas, and trim or decorative applications.
#*Section symbols to further explain the construction of any ceiling features.

#Rely on the legend to identify symbols for key ceiling features. In addition to light fixtures and ceiling fans, most RCPs identify every other type of item attached to the ceiling. Common examples include:<ref>https://www.northernarchitecture.us/building-codes/reflected-ceiling-plan.html</ref>[[Image:Read a Reflected Ceiling Plan Step 8.jpg|center]]
#*Speakers from a stereo or other communication device.
#*Emergency lighting and/or exit signs.
#*Security cameras or domes.
#*Sprinkler heads.
#*Smoke or fire alarm devices.
#*Return air grilles and supply air diffusers for the HVAC system.
#*Exhaust fans.
#*Seismic information and/or details.
#*Expansion joint information and/or details.
#*Electrical wiring between fixtures (this isn’t shown in all RCPs).
===Using the RCP Alongside Other Plans===

#Compare the RCP to the floor plan that complements it. Look at the floor plan from the same perspective—above the ceiling, with the ceiling being transparent—but forget about the mirrored floor this time. Instead, imagine that you’re looking directly down onto the floor and whatever is on or slightly above it.<ref>https://www.onland.info/archives/2017/11/reflected_ceiling_plans.php</ref>[[Image:Read a Reflected Ceiling Plan Step 5 Version 2.jpg|center]]

#*In some, but not all, RCPs, floor plan items (like furniture) appear in dashed lines, while ceiling items appear in full lines. In a coordinating floor plan, the dashed and full lines are reversed—that is, the ceiling fan symbol would be drawn with dashed lines.
#*The RCP and floor plan should be drawn at the exact same scale. Check the scale notation on the drawing to confirm this.

#Use the RCP and floor plan together to relate ceiling and floor features. For instance, using the plans together allows you to observe the relationship between the light fixtures above and the furniture below.<ref>https://www.lifeofanarchitect.com/architectural-graphics-101-number-01/</ref>[[Image:Read a Reflected Ceiling Plan Step 6.jpg|center]]

#*By using the plans together, you may determine that you need to relocate a light fixture, move furniture, or make more significant architectural or design changes. Remember, it’s much easier to do it now, on paper!

#Refer to a separate electrical plan if wiring isn’t included in the RCP. Some RCPs show the wiring runs, junction boxes, switches, and so on. However, this can cause the RCP to become very cluttered, so this information may instead be provided in a separate electrical plan. This plan, like the RCP and floor plan, should be drawn to the same scale so that all 3 can be used in concert with each other. Use the legend on the electrical plan to identify items such as:<ref>https://cdn-web.iccsafe.org/wp-content/uploads/PR-Elec-Req.pdf</ref> [[Image:Read a Reflected Ceiling Plan Step 9 Version 2.jpg|center]]
#*Electrical wiring specifications.
#*Circuitry layout.
#*Connections to the electrical panel.
#*Location of switches.
*Like other building plans, an RCP layout must comply with local building codes, electrical codes, and fire codes.

*Interior designers and architects draw reflected ceiling plans and then pass them to their consulting engineering firm. The electrical engineer then adds the electrical circuitry, etc, either on the RCP or in a separate electrical plan.
